CausalChain: Hypoxia in HCC -> HIF activation -> Upregulation of serine synthesis pathway and m6A stabilization of SSP transcripts (PHGDH, PSPH, SHMT2, etc.) -> Enhanced one‑carbon metabolism and SAM production -> Site-specific epigenetic modifications (DNA and histone methylation) -> Silencing of immune-activating/drug-sensitizing genes -> Enhanced resistance to TKIs and ICIs
Hypothesis: In hypoxic HCC, HIF activation drives both the upregulation of the serine synthesis pathway and the m6A-mediated stabilization of its key transcripts, thereby significantly boosting one‑carbon metabolism and SAM production. This increased SAM availability leads to targeted epigenetic alterations—specifically, promoter hypermethylation and changes in repressive histone marks—that silence critical immune-activating and drug-sensitizing genes. Consequently, the metabolic-epigenetic reprogramming contributes to resistance against TKIs and ICIs. We hypothesize that using advanced multi-omics approaches to map these changes, combined with CRISPR-dCas9 epigenome editing and selective metabolic inhibitors (targeting PHGDH and related enzymes), can reverse these epigenetic modifications, reactivating the expression of drug-sensitivity genes and ultimately restoring therapeutic efficacy in resistant HCC.
Abstract: We propose that in hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) activation not only upregulates the serine synthesis pathway but also, through m6A-mediated stabilization of its transcripts, amplifies one-carbon metabolism leading to increased S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) production. This surplus of SAM drives site-specific epigenetic modifications—such as promoter hypermethylation and repressive histone modifications—on key immune-activating and drug-sensitizing genes, thereby fostering resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). By leveraging contemporary multi-omics analyses and CRISPR-dCas9 based epigenome editing, we aim to dissect and therapeutically target this integrated metabolic-epigenetic axis to restore drug sensitivity. This study refines existing links by integrating m6A modifications and defining precise epigenetic marks, offering a novel and actionable framework for combating TKI/ICI resistance in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused on HIF-mediated serine synthesis leading to enhanced one‑carbon metabolism and SAM production, which then induced broad epigenetic repression of drug-sensitivity genes. The revised hypothesis retains this core causal chain but incorporates two major enhancements: (1) it adds the role of m6A-mediated transcript stabilization of SSP enzymes, as evidenced by recent studies linking m6A modifications to sorafenib resistance, and (2) it specifies the nature of the epigenetic alterations (promoter hypermethylation and repressive histone modifications) and identifies precise therapeutic modalities (e.g., CRISPR-dCas9 epigenome editing and metabolic enzyme inhibitors). These modifications address previous gaps by refining the mechanistic details and aligning the hypothesis with current technological capabilities for experimental validation and therapeutic intervention.
